title: Cohesion across sentences
summary: Use reference chains, contrast, repetition and chronology across a paragraph to recover a missing word.

sections.title: Follow a chain of meaning
content: Read this chain aloud: Farid opened the toolkit. He removed a tester from it. This allowed the repair to begin. Explain what he, it and this point back to.
A cohesive passage carries people, objects, events and time forward from one sentence to the next. A gap may therefore be impossible to solve accurately if you read only its sentence.

sections.title: Use the anchor–relation–timeline routine
content: Scan one sentence before and one sentence after the gap. Mark every repeated name, pronoun, demonstrative, time phrase and contrast word.
Locate the anchor: the person, object, action or idea that the missing word must connect to. Check number and gender when the answer is a pronoun.
Name the relation between the sentences: continuation, contrast, cause, result, repetition or time sequence. This rules out connectors that are grammatical but logically wrong.
Place the event on the paragraph timeline. Words such as then and again depend on what has already happened, so reread the completed paragraph rather than only the completed sentence.

sections.title: Prove each link from another sentence
content: Rina registers visitors and Farid examines devices. If a later sentence says that he sets down a toolkit, the male reference and the tool-related role identify Farid rather than Rina.
After a repaired lamp lights, “This encouraged the waiting visitors” uses this to refer to the whole successful event, not to a single nearby noun.
An expectation of simple repairs followed by a difficult radio creates contrast, so however or yet can link the two sentences. An addition connector would misstate their relationship.
In “Only then did he notice the loose wire”, then is justified by the tests described earlier. In “switched it on again”, again is justified only if an earlier attempt has already occurred.

sections.title: Draw the paragraph links
content: For each blank, draw an arrow to its anchor in another sentence. Label the arrow reference, contrast, repetition or chronology before proposing a word.
Test the candidate twice: first for sentence grammar, then for paragraph logic. If two words remain natural, keep both for review rather than inventing a rule that the passage does not support.

sections.title: Restore a repair-café account
content: Read all five paragraphs of “The repair café record”. Complete eight gaps whose evidence may appear before or after the blank.
After filling every gap, trace the people, objects and event sequence from the opening plan to the closing record. Change any answer that breaks a reference chain or reverses the timeline.

sections.title: Diagnose the cohesion error
content: Reference error: I linked a pronoun or demonstrative to the wrong person, object or event.
Relation error: I used addition, contrast, cause or result even though the neighbouring sentences expressed a different relationship.
Timeline error: I ignored which action happened first or whether an action was repeated.
Sentence-only error: my answer fitted the immediate grammar but contradicted evidence elsewhere in the paragraph. Record the nearest cause before retrying.

sections.title: The repair café record
content: Complete one original eight-gap account using reference chains, contrast and chronology. Feedback appears only after the complete passage is submitted.
